title: bridgenorm
text:
A batch is bridged when at least one of its reference samples has a reference_id that is also measured in the anchor batch. Connection through other batches does not count. This is the rule bn_fit uses for unbridged.

bn_bridges(samples, anchor)





samples


Data frame with columns sample_id, batch and reference_id (NA for samples that are not references).




anchor


The anchor batch. Required.

  reference_id = c("R1", "R1", "R2", NA)

title: bridgenorm
text:
For each batch, population and marker, summarises how noisy and how unusual the reference samples are, so the user can choose the anchor batch. It never chooses the anchor itself.

bn_reference_noise(
  x,
  samples,
  population,
  markers,
  transform = NULL,
  min_cells = 50,
  sample_ids = NULL
)





x


A numeric matrix (cells by markers) or a data frame with one row per cell, already transformed. A data frame needs a sample_id column unless sample_ids is given.




samples


Data frame, one row per sample: sample_id, batch, reference_id (the bridge donor; NA for study samples) and optionally aliquot.




population


Per-cell population labels, one per row of x, frozen before correction.




markers


Marker columns to correct.




transform


Optional list(name = “asinh”, cofactor = <number>): the scale x is on. It does not change the report; when given, it is checked and stored as the transform attribute of the result.




min_cells


Minimum cells per reference aliquot summary and per (batch, node) quantile table.




sample_ids


Optional sample id per row; required for a matrix x.



Columns:


n_references, n_aliquots


Reference donors and aliquots with at least min_cells cells.


replicate_sd


Pooled within-donor SD of aliquot means: \(\sqrt{\sum (m_a - \bar m_r)^2 / (n_{aliquots} - n_{references})}\). NA when no donor has two aliquots in the batch.


cell_sd


Mean over aliquots of the SD of their cells.


loo_z


Leave-one-batch-out z of the batch’s donor mean, averaged over donors: (donor mean in the batch - its mean over the other batches) / its SD over the other batches. A donor needs two other batches; NA when none has.


A donor mean is the equal-weight mean of its aliquot means, as in bn_fit_paired.

A tibble with one row per batch, population and marker.

bn_fit, bn_bridges


library("bridgenorm")

# Two batches, each with two bridge wells of one reference donor and one
# study sample. Marker M is shifted by 0.5 in batch b2; Lin separates two
# cell states.
set.seed(1)
samples <- data.frame(
  sample_id = c("r1_b1", "r2_b1", "s_b1", "r1_b2", "r2_b2", "s_b2"),
  batch = rep(c("b1", "b2"), each = 3),
  reference_id = rep(c("donor", "donor", NA), 2),
  aliquot = rep(c("a1", "a2", NA), 2)
)
x <- do.call(rbind, lapply(seq_len(nrow(samples)), function(i) {
  shift <- if (samples$batch[i] == "b2") 0.5 else 0
  data.frame(
    sample_id = samples$sample_id[i],
    Lin = c(rnorm(200, 1, 0.2), rnorm(200, 4, 0.2)),
    M = c(rnorm(200, 2, 0.3), rnorm(200, 1, 0.3)) + shift
  )
}))
bn_reference_noise(x, samples, rep("T", nrow(x)), markers = "M")

title: bridgenorm
text:
Batch effects can change the shape of a marker’s distribution within a cell state, not only its location. bn_fit() runs a node shift (.bn_fit_nodes()), then refits a second map on the shifted cells and, in each second-pass node, maps every batch’s marker quantiles onto the anchor’s.

bn_fit(
  x,
  samples,
  population,
  markers,
  transform,
  anchor,
  grid,
  mapping_markers,
  seed,
  min_cells = 50,
  unbridged = "abstain",
  train_cells = 500,
  rlen = 100,
  fallback = "global",
  quantile_probs = seq(0.025, 0.975, length.out = 21),
  shrink_k = 1000,
  target = "anchor",
  goal_batches = NULL,
  sample_ids = NULL,
  shrink_target = "value",
  shrink_reweight = FALSE,
  quantile_maps = TRUE
)





x


A numeric matrix (cells by markers) or a data frame with one row per cell, already transformed. A data frame needs a sample_id column unless sample_ids is given.




samples


Data frame, one row per sample: sample_id, batch, reference_id (the bridge donor; NA for study samples) and optionally aliquot.




population


Per-cell population labels, one per row of x, frozen before correction.




markers


Marker columns to correct.




transform


list(name = “asinh”, cofactor = <number>): the scale x is on. It is recorded, never applied.




anchor


The batch that defines the target scale.




grid


SOM grid as c(xdim, ydim).




mapping_markers


Markers that define cell state for the map; each must be one of markers.




seed


Seed for the training-cell draw and the SOM.




min_cells


Minimum cells per reference aliquot summary and per (batch, node) quantile table.




unbridged


“abstain” leaves a batch that shares no bridge donor with the anchor raw and flags it; “stop” refuses the fit.




train_cells


Maximum training cells per reference sample for the SOM.




rlen


Number of SOM training passes (kohonen::som).




fallback


For a (batch, node, marker) without a node effect: “global” takes the batch’s global shift, “abstain” keeps the raw value.




quantile_probs


Increasing probabilities in (0, 1), at least two, at which batch and anchor quantiles are matched.




shrink_k


Non-negative pseudo-count of cells for the shrinkage toward the batch-wide offset curve. Larger values borrow more; 0 turns shrinkage off. “eb” estimates one pseudo-count per marker by empirical Bayes from how much node offsets vary beyond their sampling noise, never below 300; the values are stored in settings$shrink_k_marker. It is kept for study; in benchmarks it did not beat the scalar default.




target


“anchor” corrects every batch to the anchor batch. “virtual” corrects every batch, the anchor included, to a virtual reference: per reference summary and per SOM node, the equal-weight mean over batches (for quantiles, the mean of the batches’ quantile curves). It covers the same summaries and nodes as the anchor, which still sets the bridges and the map. Not combined with shrink_k = “eb”.




goal_batches


NULL, or with target = “virtual” two or more batches whose equal-weight mean is the goal (for example the batches of one study), as CytoNorm’s goal distribution. Goal batches that are unbridged or whose reference donors differ from the anchor’s are dropped. The anchor still sets the bridges and the map and may lie outside the goal; the fit stops when the goal lacks a reference summary the anchor has. Nodes without a goal quantile table take the pass-2 node shift.




sample_ids


Optional sample id per row; required for a matrix x.




shrink_target


What each node’s offset curve is shrunk toward. “value” (default since 1.1.0) evaluates the batch-wide map (the batch’s quantile function composed with the target’s distribution function) at the node’s own target quantiles, so an intensity-dependent effect that is the same in every node is not shrunk toward a wrong curve. Beyond the outer batch-wide quantiles the map moves by their difference. “quantile” (the 1.0.0 behaviour) adds the batch-wide offset at the same probability, which equals the node’s offset only under a pure location shift. The value is stored in settings$shrink_target.




shrink_reweight


FALSE (default), or TRUE to compute the batch-wide curve with cell weights that give the batch the target’s share of reference cells in every second-pass node (the anchor’s, or with target = “virtual” the mean over the goal batches). It matters when a batch’s bridge samples have a different cell-state mix than the target’s.




quantile_maps


TRUE (default), or FALSE to keep no quantile tables, so every cell takes the pass-2 node shift (an ablation).



Steps, all on reference cells only:


Pass 1: .bn_fit_nodes() with the given settings; its correction is applied to the reference cells.


Pass 2: .bn_fit_nodes() again, with the same settings, on the pass-1 cells. Its node shifts cover the cells pass 2 cannot map by quantiles.


For each (batch, pass-2 node) with at least min_cells reference cells pooled over its reference samples, in a batch whose reference donors (reference_id) are exactly the anchor’s, the quantiles at quantile_probs of every marker (stats::quantile(), type 7) are stored.


Shrinkage: in each such (batch, node) of a non-anchor batch whose node also has anchor quantiles, the node’s batch quantiles are pulled toward what the batch-wide map (built from all the batch’s pass-1 reference cells and the anchor’s) predicts for the node, with weight \(n / (n + shrink_k)\) on the node’s own quantiles, \(n\) being the batch’s reference cells in the node. With shrink_target = “value” (default) the batch-wide map is read at the node’s anchor quantiles; with “quantile” the batch-wide offset at the same probability is added to them. Each column of a shrunk table is then sorted (rearrangement; Chernozhukov, Fernandez-Val and Galichon 2010), because the mix can cross itself. shrink_k = 0 keeps the fitted tables.


At integrate time, pass 1 is applied, then each cell is assigned to its nearest pass-2 node. If its batch and the anchor both have quantiles in that node, each marker value is mapped by linear interpolation from the batch’s quantiles to the anchor’s; beyond the outer quantiles it moves by the difference of the outer quantiles (tail = “shift”). Other cells take the pass-2 node shift. Anchor cells are mapped onto their own quantiles, which leaves values between the outer quantiles unchanged.
A batch with other reference donors than the anchor has no quantiles: pooled distributions of different donors differ by biology, not only by batch. Such a batch takes the pass-2 node shift if it is bridged, and is left raw if it is not.
The quantile rule pools wells, while the node shifts count cells per reference sample; a (batch, node) can therefore have quantiles without a node shift.

A bn_node_quantile_model: a list with schema_version, settings, markers, transform, anchor, pass1 and pass2 (frozen node models), quantiles (one probabilities-by-markers matrix per batch and node; the list names are internal keys), software, created, parent_digest and digest.

The defaults come from benchmarking: min_cells = 50, train_cells = 500, rlen = 100, 21 quantiles from 0.025 to 0.975, shrink_k = 1000 with shrink_target = “value” (since 1.1.0; 1.0.0 used 300 and “quantile”). Check them on new data. grid, mapping_markers, anchor and seed have no default.

# study sample. Marker M is shifted by 0.5 in batch b2; Lin separates two
# cell states.
set.seed(1)
samples <- data.frame(
  sample_id = c("r1_b1", "r2_b1", "s_b1", "r1_b2", "r2_b2", "s_b2"),
  batch = rep(c("b1", "b2"), each = 3),
  reference_id = rep(c("donor", "donor", NA), 2),
  aliquot = rep(c("a1", "a2", NA), 2)
)
x <- do.call(rbind, lapply(seq_len(nrow(samples)), function(i) {
  shift <- if (samples$batch[i] == "b2") 0.5 else 0
  data.frame(
    sample_id = samples$sample_id[i],
    Lin = c(rnorm(200, 1, 0.2), rnorm(200, 4, 0.2)),
    M = c(rnorm(200, 2, 0.3), rnorm(200, 1, 0.3)) + shift
  )
}))
model <- bn_fit(
  x, samples, population = rep("T", nrow(x)), markers = c("Lin", "M"),
  transform = list(name = "asinh", cofactor = 5), anchor = "b1",
  grid = c(2, 1), mapping_markers = "Lin", seed = 1, rlen = 20
)

title: bridgenorm
text:
Batch correction for cytometry from bridge samples: reference material from the same donor measured in every batch.
Site and articles: https://mdmanurung.github.io/bridgenorm/
The differences between bridge samples measure the technical batch effect. bridgenorm estimates the batch effect from them alone: study samples never enter a fit, so a condition that is confounded with batch cannot shape the correction. Each batch is corrected toward one anchor batch, or toward the mean of a chosen set of batches. A fitted model is frozen with a digest, so it applies to new data without changing earlier corrections.



bridgenorm workflow: bridge samples in every batch, a model fitted on bridge cells only, then applied to every cell




bn_fit() is the main method. It works on reference cells only, in two passes:

A global paired shift places the bridge cells, and a self-organising map (SOM) on the mapping markers splits them into nodes (cell states). Each batch gets a paired shift per node: the mean over shared bridge donors of the batch-minus-anchor donor means.
The global shift, map and node shifts are refitted on the pass-1 cells. In each (batch, node), the batch’s marker quantiles are mapped onto the anchor’s; cells without a map take the pass-2 node shift. This corrects changes in the shape of a distribution, not only its location. Every node’s map is shrunk toward the batch-wide map, keeping weight n / (n + shrink_k) on its own, so small nodes borrow most. Since 1.1.0 the batch-wide map is read at the node’s own values (shrink_target = "value", shrink_k = 1000), so a stretch shared by all nodes is kept.




The two passes inside bn_fit(): SOM nodes and paired shifts, a refitted map, per-node quantile maps, and shrinkage of small nodes


Only batches whose bridge donors equal the anchor’s get quantile maps; other bridged batches get node shifts only, and bn_fit() warns which. A batch that shares no bridge donor with the anchor is left raw, and bn_apply() says so.
These options are off by default.

target = "virtual" corrects every batch, the anchor included, toward a virtual reference. Per SOM node, the reference is the equal-weight mean of the batches’ quantile curves. text:
bn_fit() is the main method. It works on reference cells only, in two passes:

A global paired shift places the bridge cells, and a self-organising map (SOM) on the mapping markers splits them into nodes (cell states). Each batch gets a paired shift per node: the mean over shared bridge donors of the batch-minus-anchor donor means.
The global shift, map and node shifts are refitted on the pass-1 cells. Since 1.1.0 the batch-wide map is read at the node’s own values (shrink_target = "value", shrink_k = 1000), so a stretch shared by all nodes is kept.

title: Use case 3: Correct later batches with a frozen model
text:
Longitudinal clinical studies run for months or years. Samples are measured as subjects come in, and an interim analysis often starts before the last batch is measured. If every new batch changed the correction of earlier ones, every interim result would have to be redone. A bridgenorm model is frozen: bn_apply() corrects a new batch from its own bridge wells, against the anchor summaries stored in the model, and leaves the earlier batches exactly as they were.
The price is that a late batch gets node shifts only, not quantile maps: the maps need the batch’s bridge cells at fit time. For the final analysis, refit on all batches.

title: Compare with CytoNorm and cyCombine on simulated data
text: This article compares bridgenorm with two widely used batch-correction tools, CytoNorm and cyCombine, on simulated data where the truth is known. The study design and the size of the batch effects are set to realistic values for a multi-batch cytometry study with bridge samples. The methods were run once with the script tools/sim-compare.R in the package repository; the article reads its saved results, so building it does not need CytoNorm or cyCombine.
crumbs: Compare with CytoNorm and cyCombine on simulated data

title: Compare with CytoNorm and cyCombine on simulated data
text:
Simulated data
Each data set has 15 batches. The first batch is the anchor and carries no batch effect. Every batch holds 3 (2 fit, 1 held out) bridge aliquots of one reference donor and 12 study samples from different donors, with 5000 cells per sample. Cells come from 8 populations measured on 24 markers. Study donors differ in population mix and carry small marker offsets. Cases carry a known condition effect: +0.4 on M05 in population P3.
Two kinds of batch effect are simulated:


Global shift: one shift per batch and marker, the same for every cell. Its size varies by marker; the median standard deviation over batches is 0.084.

Calibrated: the global shift plus, per batch, population and marker, a further shift (median SD 0.1) and a stretch or compression of the distribution (median SD of the log scale factor 0.236). The batch effect then differs between cell states and changes the shape of the distributions. The three spreads were measured on bridge wells of an unpublished multi-batch study with bridgenorm at shrink_k = 0; the scale spread is an upper estimate, because it also holds sampling noise.

And two study designs:


Balanced: six cases and six controls in every batch.

Confounded: from 1 to 11 cases per batch (1, 2, 2, 3, 4, 5, 5, 6, 7, 7, 8, 9, 10, 10, 11), so condition and batch overlap.

That makes four scenarios, each simulated with ten seeds; every simulated data set is corrected with three SOM seeds, so each method has 30 replicates per scenario. A last arm keeps the simulated values without batch effect: the floor that sampling noise sets for every score.

title: Compare with CytoNorm and cyCombine on simulated data
text:
Methods and settings
All methods use the same 8 by 8 self-organising map grid; otherwise each runs with its package defaults. bridgenorm and CytoNorm are fitted on two of the three bridge aliquots of every batch; the third is held out for scoring. cyCombine has no separate apply step; it is fitted on and corrects all cells, study samples and the held-out aliquot included, as it is designed to. cyCombine runs twice: with its default of no covariate, and with the true condition (case or control) as covariate, which is what its documentation suggests when the condition is known. That second run uses labels that the bridge-based methods never see. The paired shift (bn_fit_paired(), one shift per batch and marker) is the baseline.
crumbs: Compare with CytoNorm and cyCombine on simulated data

title: Compare with CytoNorm and cyCombine on simulated data
text:
How the methods are scored


Held-out bridge EMD measures how much batch effect is left. The held-out bridge aliquot is the same donor in every batch, so after a perfect correction its distributions match across batches. Per marker, the score takes the largest one-dimensional earth mover’s distance between any two of the 15 batches, then the median over markers. Lower is better. Sampling noise alone keeps the score above zero.

Condition-effect recovery measures whether biology survives. Per study sample, the median of the effect marker in the effect population is taken; the effect is the mean of cases minus the mean of controls, with no batch term. The figures show the estimate divided by the true effect, so 1 means the effect is kept.
crumbs: Compare with CytoNorm and cyCombine on simulated data

title: Compare with CytoNorm and cyCombine on simulated data
text:
Batch effect left after correction








Points are the 30 replicates; bars are their mean. The design changes only the study samples, so the bridge-based scores repeat across the two designs.
Global shift. CytoNorm (0.048), bridgenorm (0.052) and the paired shift (0.054) bring the held-out EMD down from 0.298 to nearly the same level; cyCombine leaves slightly more (0.056). A global shift is what the paired shift is built for, so the node-level methods gain little here.
Calibrated batch effect. The paired shift now falls behind (0.144), because one shift per batch and marker cannot follow effects that differ between cell states. CytoNorm leaves the least (0.049), then bridgenorm (0.058) and cyCombine (0.073 without, 0.069 with the covariate). CytoNorm and bridgenorm both learn per-cluster quantile maps from the bridge samples. bridgenorm also pulls each node’s map toward the batch-wide map: with about 150 bridge cells per node here and the default shrink_k = 1000, a node keeps about an eighth of its own map. That explains part of why it leaves more of the cell-state-specific effect than CytoNorm: with shrink_k = 0, the held-out EMD here falls to 0.052.
The defaults changed in bridgenorm 1.1.0, from shrinkage toward the batch-wide curve at the same quantile with shrink_k = 300 (“bridgenorm 1.0.0” in the figures) to shrinkage toward the batch-wide map at the same value with shrink_k = 1000. They were chosen by tuning on held-out bridge wells of two real studies, which are not public. In these simulations the change is a trade-off. Under the calibrated batch effect, the 1.1.0 defaults lower the held-out EMD (from 0.066 to 0.058, lower in 30 of 30 replicates), but raise the error of study cells against their values without batch effect (from 0.067 to 0.071, higher in 30 of 30). Under the global shift the two scores move the other way, and less. Counting a win only when a method is better in every replicate, CytoNorm beats bridgenorm on held-out EMD under the calibrated batch effect: it is lower in 30 of 30 replicates.

title: Compare with CytoNorm and cyCombine on simulated data
text:
Biology kept after correction








Balanced design. With the condition balanced within every batch, a batch effect does not bias the case-control difference much, and every method stays close to the truth.
Confounded design. Here cases sit mostly in some batches, so any batch effect left in the data, or any biology removed as batch effect, biases the estimate.

Under the calibrated batch effect, the uncorrected estimate is 0.88 to 1.27 times the true effect. bridgenorm (0.96 to 1.12) and CytoNorm (0.97 to 1.14) bring it near 1; the paired shift less so (0.91 to 1.20).
cyCombine without a covariate shrinks the effect (0.68 to 0.86 under the global shift, 0.78 to 1.07 under the calibrated one). It is fitted on the study samples, and when cases cluster in some batches, part of the case effect looks like batch effect and is removed.
With the true condition as covariate, cyCombine keeps the effect (0.89 to 1.09 and 0.98 to 1.21), but only because it is told which samples are cases.

Methods that learn the batch effect from bridge samples only never see the condition, so a confounded design cannot pull the condition into their correction.
CytoNorm maps every batch to the mean of all batches by default, while bridgenorm maps to the anchor batch; the effect ratio is read on each method’s own scale. With its goal set to the anchor batch, CytoNorm’s estimate under the calibrated batch effect moves from 1.065 to 1.019 times the true effect (bridgenorm 1.044), so most of CytoNorm’s excess came from its target. On the error of each study cell against its value without batch effect, CytoNorm with the anchor goal is closer than bridgenorm in 30 of 30 replicates under the calibrated batch effect (mean 0.049 against 0.071).

title: Compare with CytoNorm and cyCombine on simulated data
text:
Longitudinal study with repeated visits
Clinical studies often sample each subject at several visits, and the visits land in different batches. This section simulates that design to ask whether correction keeps a within-subject change over time. It uses the same simulator, calibration and batches as above, with a staggered design: each batch holds the first visit (t1) of a new cohort of four subjects, the second visit (t2) of the previous cohort and the third visit (t3) of the cohort before that. Thirteen cohorts give 52 subjects over the fifteen batches, so visit and batch overlap within every subject. In one population, one marker rises by 0.2 at t2 and 0.4 at t3; no other marker changes. Each subject keeps one population mix and marker offset across visits, plus small visit-to-visit noise. Both batch effects were simulated with ten seeds, each corrected with three SOM seeds (30 replicates); the script is tools/sim-longitudinal.R.
CytoNorm runs three times here: with its default 15 by 15 grid, with the 8 by 8 grid shared by the other methods, and with its default grid and the anchor batch as goal. Six scores are reported, with no single primary one:


Effect error at t2 and t3: the mean within-subject change of the effect marker in the effect population, divided by the true change; the score is the distance from 1.

Drift on no-change markers: the median, over the other markers, of the absolute mean change from t1 to t3. The truth is 0.

Noise SD on no-change markers: the median, over the other markers, of the standard deviation across subjects of the t1-to-t3 change. Batch effect left in the data adds to this noise.

Paired t of the t3 effect: the mean change over its standard error, a measure of how easily a study would detect the effect.

Held-out bridge EMD, as above.









Points are the 30 replicates; bars are their mean. Drift and noise SD are on the no-change markers. Lower is better for every score except the paired t.
In this staggered design, the time effect survives every method, including no correction. Each subject’s visits sit in three consecutive batches, and different subjects meet different batches, so batch effects largely cancel in the mean change. Uncorrected data estimate the t3 effect at 1.061 times the truth under the calibrated batch effect.
What correction buys is precision. Under the calibrated batch effect, the batch effect left in uncorrected data inflates the subject-to-subject noise (0.204) and keeps the paired t at 13. bridgenorm cuts the noise to 0.063 and CytoNorm to 0.066, raising the paired t to 35 and 44. The paired shift gets part of the way (t = 19).
In this design, bridgenorm and CytoNorm keep time effects about equally well, and neither wins across scores. Counting a win only when a method is better in all 30 replicates, bridgenorm against the three CytoNorm settings has 0 wins, 0 losses and 36 ties over the 36 comparisons. bridgenorm has the lower noise under the calibrated batch effect. CytoNorm aligns the held-out bridge aliquot better under the calibrated batch effect (0.050 against 0.056), and its mean paired t is higher, though not in every replicate. The three CytoNorm settings score almost the same. With shrink_k = 0, bridgenorm’s paired t under the calibrated batch effect rises to 44 and its held-out EMD falls to 0.052, but its noise rises to 0.066. Against the 1.0.0 defaults, the 1.1.0 defaults win only on held-out EMD under the calibrated batch effect and tie on every time-effect score; their mean paired t there is 35 against 37.
Harder designs: drift and visits confounded with batch
The staggered design is kind: every subject meets different batches at each visit, so batch effects cancel in the mean change. Four harder designs test what can go wrong, all under the calibrated batch effect:


Instrument drift: every sample, bridge and study alike, reads two markers (the effect marker M05 and a no-change marker M10) higher by 0.05 per batch, on top of the batch effect.

Visit confounded with batch: all first visits run in batches 1 to 5, second visits in 6 to 10 and third visits in 11 to 15.

Bridge drift: the bridge material itself changes, by 0.02 per batch on M05 and M10; the study samples do not.

Confounded + bridge drift: both.

The time effect is now estimated with a mixed model of the per-sample medians, with a random intercept per subject, and again with a random intercept per batch added, as a downstream analysis might.








Points are the 30 replicates; bars are their mean; dashed lines mark the truth.
Drift of the instrument is removed; drift of the bridge material is not. Under instrument drift, uncorrected data overstate the M05 effect (1.31 times the truth), and every correction brings it back (bridgenorm 1.01, CytoNorm 1.05). When the bridge material drifts instead, every bridge-based correction reads the drift as batch effect and subtracts it from the study samples. The effect shrinks (bridgenorm 0.90, CytoNorm 0.94), and the no-change marker M10 gains a false change (bridgenorm -0.043, against -0.005 uncorrected).
Confounding visit with batch makes bridge drift much worse. With visits in separate blocks of batches, the M05 effect falls to 0.50 of the truth for bridgenorm and 0.52 for CytoNorm, and M10 shows a false change of -0.207. Without bridge drift the same blocked design is safe after correction (bridgenorm 1.00).
A batch term in the downstream model does not repair it. With visit and batch confounded, a batch term cannot separate drift from time; in the staggered designs it recovers only a little. The protection is in the design: keep one bridge lot, check it for drift, and spread each subject’s visits over batches.

A second check uses the BatchVaria package, which splits the variance of per-sample features into the share explained by batch, by the condition (or by visit and subject in the longitudinal designs), and the rest. The table gives the percent of variance explained by batch, for the median of each marker in each simulated population of the study samples, as the mean over three simulation seeds; lower is better. The no-batch-effect column is the floor: samples differ by chance, so batch explains a little even without a batch effect. The script is tools/eval-batchvaria.R; it also scores the medians in each node of a shared 5 by 5 SOM, with the same order of methods.
bridgenorm with the 1.0.0 defaults and CytoNorm leave about the same share. The 1.1.0 defaults leave slightly more in every scenario (15.3 against 13.5 percent under the calibrated batch effect), in line with their higher error against the truth. cyCombine falls below the floor (0.9 against 7.7 percent under the global shift): it is fitted on the study samples, so it likely removes chance differences between batches along with the batch effect.

title: Compare with CytoNorm and cyCombine on simulated data
text:
Limits of this comparison

The simulation was written by the bridgenorm author and follows bridgenorm’s design: one reference donor in every batch, and an anchor batch without batch effect. Its batch effects are shifts and linear stretches within populations.
The held-out bridge score suits methods that learn from bridge samples. cyCombine is scored on cells it was fitted on, and it targets the mean of all batches rather than the bridge donor.
In the cross-sectional comparison each method ran with one setting per tool on a shared 8 by 8 grid, which is not the CytoNorm default of 15 by 15; the longitudinal section also runs CytoNorm at 15 by 15.
CytoNorm maps every batch to the mean of all batches and cyCombine to the mean of all cells, while bridgenorm maps to the anchor batch. The effect ratio is read on each method’s own target scale.
Ten simulation seeds crossed with three SOM seeds per cross-sectional scenario, and five per longitudinal one, give ranges, not confidence intervals.
cyCombine’s bridge options (ref.batch with anchor) were tried and dropped: its per-cluster ComBat stops when a cluster has no cell of the reference batch, which happened in most runs.
The longitudinal simulation has four subjects per cohort, one changing marker in one population, and visits in consecutive batches. Studies with visits far apart in time, or with bridge material that ages, may behave differently.
cyCombine and the bridge-based methods answer different questions. cyCombine removes differences between batches of all cells; bridgenorm and CytoNorm remove only what the bridge samples show. Which is right depends on whether biology can differ between batches.

title: Use case 2: Normalize toward a goal distribution
text:
By default bridgenorm corrects every batch toward one anchor batch. That is not always the target you want. A study may be run in two phases, and the later phase should be put on the scale of the earlier one, so the earlier analysis (gates, clusters, thresholds) still holds. Or one anchor batch may be noisy, and the mean of several batches is a steadier target. CytoNorm offers this through its goal distribution: the mean over batches by default, one goal batch, or goal quantiles from an earlier model.
bridgenorm has the same choices:


target = "anchor" (the default): the goal is the anchor batch.

target = "virtual": the goal is the equal-weight mean of all batches. In each SOM node, the goal quantile curve is the mean of the batches’ curves; for the paired shift, each bridge summary is the mean over batches.

target = "virtual", goal_batches = <batches>: the goal is the equal-weight mean of the given batches only.

The anchor still sets the bridges and the map, and it may lie outside the goal batches. Batches in goal_batches that are unbridged, or whose bridge donors differ from the anchor’s, are dropped from the goal. No benchmark benefit of a goal over the anchor target is claimed yet; use it when the design asks for it.
crumbs: Use case 2: Normalize toward a goal distribution

title: Use case 2: Normalize toward a goal distribution
text:
Prepare the bridgenorm normalization step

library(bridgenorm)

Six batches come from two studies: study 1 ran batches b1 to b3, study 2 batches b4 to b6. Each batch holds two bridge wells of one reference donor and two study samples. Between the studies the instrument changed, so all study 2 batches read marker M higher, by 0.6 in cell state A and 0.4 in state B. On top of that, each batch shifts and stretches M by a small amount of its own. We want every batch on the scale of study 2, so the goal is the mean of b4, b5 and b6. The anchor is b1, which lies outside the goal.

set.seed(2)
batches <- paste0("b", 1:6)
centre <- c(A = 2, B = 1)
lin <- c(A = 1, B = 4)
study_shift <- c(A = 0.6, B = 0.4) # study 2 reads M higher
effect <- lapply(setNames(batches, batches), function(b) {
  in_study2 <- b %in% c("b4", "b5", "b6")
  list(
    shift = in_study2 * study_shift + c(A = rnorm(1, 0, 0.1), B = rnorm(1, 0, 0.1)),
    scale = exp(rnorm(1, 0, 0.1))
  )
})
samples <- data.frame(
  sample_id = c(outer(c("ref1", "ref2", "s1", "s2"), batches, paste, sep = "_")),
  batch = rep(batches, each = 4),
  reference_id = rep(c("donor", "donor", NA, NA), 6),
  aliquot = rep(c("ref1", "ref2", NA, NA), 6)
)
samples$study <- ifelse(samples$batch %in% c("b1", "b2", "b3"), "study1", "study2")
cells <- do.call(rbind, lapply(seq_len(nrow(samples)), function(i) {
  b <- samples$batch[i]
  do.call(rbind, lapply(c("A", "B"), function(k) {
    truth <- rnorm(300, centre[[k]], 0.3)
    data.frame(
      sample_id = samples$sample_id[i],
      Lin = rnorm(300, lin[[k]], 0.2),
      M = centre[[k]] + effect[[b]]$scale * (truth - centre[[k]]) + effect[[b]]$shift[[k]]
    )
  }))
}))
cells$batch <- samples$batch[match(cells$sample_id, samples$sample_id)]
is_bridge <- !is.na(samples$reference_id[match(cells$sample_id, samples$sample_id)])

The goal batches are all batches of study 2:

goal <- unique(samples$batch[samples$study == "study2"])
goal
#> [1] "b4" "b5" "b6"

title: Use case 2: Normalize toward a goal distribution
text:
Train the bridgenorm models
One model per goal, so the three targets can be compared: the anchor b1, the mean of all batches, and the mean of study 2.

fit <- function(...) {
  bn_fit(
    x = cells[, c("sample_id", "Lin", "M")],
    samples = samples,
    population = rep("T", nrow(cells)),
    markers = c("Lin", "M"),
    transform = list(name = "asinh", cofactor = 5),
    anchor = "b1",
    grid = c(2, 1),
    mapping_markers = "Lin",
    seed = 1,
    train_cells = 300,
    rlen = 50,
    ...
  )
}
models <- list(
  anchor = fit(),
  all_batches = fit(target = "virtual"),
  study2 = fit(target = "virtual", goal_batches = goal)
)
models$study2$settings$goal_batches
#> [1] "b4" "b5" "b6"

The goal is recorded in the model and covered by its digest, so a saved model says which batches it normalizes toward.

title: Use case 2: Normalize toward a goal distribution
text:
Evaluate the quality
Density plots
The density of M in the bridge cells of each batch (study 1 in reds, study 2 in blues), with the goal distribution in purple: the pooled bridge cells of the goal batches before correction, each batch weighted equally. Toward the anchor, every batch moves to study 1’s scale; toward the mean of all batches, every batch lands between the studies; toward the study 2 goal, every batch, study 1 included, moves onto the purple curve.

colours <- setNames(c("#900002", "#E66100", "#FFB000", "#0046A1", "#3C9BE6", "#6FCFFF"), batches)
goal_cells <- unlist(lapply(goal, function(b) {
  sample(cells$M[is_bridge & cells$batch == b], 600)
}))
op <- par(mfrow = c(2, 2), mar = c(4, 4, 2, 1))
panels <- list(uncorrected = cells$M, anchor = corrected$anchor, `all batches` = corrected$all_batches,
  `study 2 goal` = corrected$study2)
for (panel in names(panels)) {
  plot(NULL, xlim = c(-0.5, 4), ylim = c(0, 1.6), xlab = "M", ylab = "Density", main = panel)
  for (b in batches) lines(density(panels[[panel]][is_bridge & cells$batch == b]), col = colours[[b]])
  lines(density(goal_cells), col = "#7209B7", lwd = 2.5)
}
legend("topright", legend = c(batches, "goal"), col = c(colours, "#7209B7"), lwd = c(rep(1, 6), 2.5),
  bty = "n", cex = 0.8)






par(op)

Distance to the goal
The earth mover’s distance (EMD) between each batch’s corrected bridge cells and the goal distribution; lower means closer to the goal. Only the model with the study 2 goal is meant to bring every batch to it; the other two are shown for contrast. Bridge cells were used to fit the models, so this checks that the goal was reached, not how well the correction generalizes; held-out bridge wells do that (see the comparison article).

emd <- function(a, b) mean(abs(quantile(a, ppoints(200)) - quantile(b, ppoints(200))))
to_goal <- sapply(c(list(uncorrected = cells$M), corrected), function(v) {
  sapply(setNames(batches, batches), function(b) emd(v[is_bridge & cells$batch == b], goal_cells))
})
round(to_goal, 3)
#>    uncorrected anchor all_batches study2
#> b1       0.477  0.477       0.240  0.018
#> b2       0.543  0.477       0.240  0.017
#> b3       0.426  0.479       0.243  0.018
#> b4       0.047  0.475       0.239  0.019
#> b5       0.080  0.478       0.241  0.018
#> b6       0.088  0.478       0.241  0.018

Quantile-map plots
In each node, the study 2 model maps every batch’s quantiles onto the goal’s: the mean of the goal batches’ quantile curves, stored under the virtual key. The maps sit close to the diagonal because the tables are on the pass-1 scale: the pass-1 node shift has already moved every batch to the goal’s location, and the maps correct what is left of each batch’s shape.

q <- models$study2$quantiles
key_batch <- sub("\r.*", "", names(q))
key_node <- sub(".*\r", "", names(q))
virtual <- unique(key_batch[!key_batch %in% batches])
op <- par(mfrow = c(1, 2), mar = c(4, 4, 2, 1))
for (node in unique(key_node)) {
  goal_q <- q[[which(key_batch == virtual & key_node == node)]][, "M"]
  node_q <- unlist(lapply(q[key_node == node], function(x) x[, "M"]))
  plot(NULL, xlim = range(node_q), ylim = range(goal_q),
    xlab = "Batch quantiles of M", ylab = "Goal quantiles of M", main = node)
  abline(0, 1, col = "grey70", lty = 2)
  for (b in batches) {
    i <- which(key_batch == b & key_node == node)
    if (length(i) == 1) lines(q[[i]][, "M"], goal_q, col = colours[[b]], type = "b", pch = 20)
  }
}






par(op)

title: Use case 2: Normalize toward a goal distribution
text:
Notes

A goal set of one batch is the anchor target: use target = "anchor" with that batch as anchor.
When the anchor lies outside the goal, the goal must measure every bridge summary the anchor has (each reference donor, population and marker); otherwise bn_fit() stops with a message rather than produce a missing target.

bn_fit_paired() takes the same target and goal_batches arguments.
To add later batches to an existing goal without changing earlier corrections, keep the model and apply it (use case 3).

title: Use case 1: Correct batches with bridge samples
text:
In a multi-batch cytometry study, the same reference material (a bridge sample) is measured in every batch. The differences between the bridge samples measure the technical batch effect. bridgenorm estimates the batch effect from the bridge cells alone and corrects every batch toward one anchor batch. Study samples never enter the fit, so a condition that is confounded with batch cannot shape the correction. The fitted model is frozen with a digest, so it can be applied to new data later without changing earlier corrections (use case 3).

bn_fit() works in two passes. A global paired shift places the bridge cells on a self-organising map (SOM), and a paired shift is estimated per node. The shift, map and node shifts are refitted on the shifted cells. In each batch and node, the batch’s marker quantiles are then mapped onto the anchor’s, and each node’s map is shrunk toward the batch-wide map, small nodes most.

The data here are simulated, so every cell’s value without the batch effect is known and the correction can be checked against the truth.
crumbs: Use case 1: Correct batches with bridge samples

title: Use case 1: Correct batches with bridge samples
text:
Prepare the bridgenorm normalization step
Load bridgenorm

library(bridgenorm)

Organize the data
bridgenorm takes one table of cells and one table of samples. The cell table has a sample_id column and one column per marker, already transformed (here the values are on an asinh-like scale). The sample table has one row per sample: sample_id, batch, reference_id (the bridge donor, NA for study samples) and optionally aliquot (the bridge well).
Three batches each hold two bridge wells of one reference donor and two study samples. Cells fall in two cell states, A and B, separated on the marker Lin. Marker M carries the batch effect: in batch b2 it is shifted and compressed, in batch b3 shifted and stretched, and batch b1 is the anchor without an effect. The effect differs between the two cell states, so one shift per batch cannot remove it.

set.seed(1)
centre <- c(A = 2, B = 1)
lin <- c(A = 1, B = 4)
effect <- list(
  b1 = list(shift = c(A = 0, B = 0), scale = 1),
  b2 = list(shift = c(A = 0.4, B = -0.3), scale = 0.6),
  b3 = list(shift = c(A = -0.2, B = 0.3), scale = 1.4)
)
samples <- data.frame(
  sample_id = c(outer(c("ref1", "ref2", "s1", "s2"), c("b1", "b2", "b3"), paste, sep = "_")),
  batch = rep(c("b1", "b2", "b3"), each = 4),
  reference_id = rep(c("donor", "donor", NA, NA), 3),
  aliquot = rep(c("ref1", "ref2", NA, NA), 3)
)
cells <- do.call(rbind, lapply(seq_len(nrow(samples)), function(i) {
  b <- samples$batch[i]
  do.call(rbind, lapply(c("A", "B"), function(k) {
    truth <- rnorm(300, centre[[k]], 0.3)
    data.frame(
      sample_id = samples$sample_id[i],
      state = k,
      Lin = rnorm(300, lin[[k]], 0.2),
      M = centre[[k]] + effect[[b]]$scale * (truth - centre[[k]]) + effect[[b]]$shift[[k]],
      truth = truth
    )
  }))
}))
cells$batch <- samples$batch[match(cells$sample_id, samples$sample_id)]
head(cells)

#> 1   ref1_b1     A 1.1787347 1.812064 1.812064    b1

#> 4   ref1_b1     A 0.9232736 2.478584 2.478584    b1

Check the bridges and choose the anchor
Every batch must share a bridge donor with the anchor. bn_bridges() checks this; bn_reference_noise() reports how noisy each batch’s bridge wells are, to help choose the anchor (the least noisy batch is a good choice).

bn_bridges(samples, anchor = "b1")

#>   batch n_shared_with_anchor shared_ids bridged
#>   <chr>                <int> <chr>      <lgl>  
#> 1 b2                       1 donor      TRUE   
#> 2 b3                       1 donor      TRUE
bn_reference_noise(cells[, c("sample_id", "M")], samples, rep("T", nrow(cells)), markers = "M")
#> # A tibble: 3 × 8
#>   batch population marker n_references n_aliquots replicate_sd cell_sd   loo_z

title: Use case 1: Correct batches with bridge samples
text:
Train the bridgenorm model
The model is fitted on bridge cells only. The anchor, the SOM grid, the mapping markers, the seed and the transform depend on the data and must be given. The other settings have benchmarked defaults; here the SOM training is shortened for the toy data. mapping_markers define the cell states; every marker in markers is corrected, whether or not it is used for mapping.

model <- bn_fit(
  x = cells[, c("sample_id", "Lin", "M")],
  samples = samples,
  population = rep("T", nrow(cells)),
  markers = c("Lin", "M"),
  transform = list(name = "asinh", cofactor = 5),
  anchor = "b1",
  grid = c(2, 1),
  mapping_markers = "Lin",
  seed = 1,
  train_cells = 300, # this toy data has 600 cells per sample
  rlen = 50
)
model
#> <bn_node_quantile_model> | anchor: b1 | nodes per pass: 2 | quantile tables: 6 | digest: a56b4bf471543651276ccdbcc4768777

population sets the strata of the global pre-shift and of the fallback for cells whose node has no effect. One label for all cells, as here, is valid.

title: Use case 1: Correct batches with bridge samples
text:
Apply the bridgenorm model
bn_apply() applies the frozen model to all cells, study samples included.

res <- bn_apply(model, cells[, c("sample_id", "Lin", "M")], samples, rep("T", nrow(cells)))

res$x holds the corrected data in the input’s shape and row order. res$actions says what was done for every pass, batch, node and marker, and why. Rows reading abstain kept raw values; bn_apply() also sends a message when a whole batch was left raw. Check it before using the result.

table(res$actions$batch, res$actions$reason_code)
#>     
#>      frozen_effect node_quantile
#>   b1             4             4
#>   b2             4             4
#>   b3             4             4

title: Use case 1: Correct batches with bridge samples
text:
Evaluate the quality
Density plots
The density of M in study cells per batch, before and after correction. After correction, batches b2 and b3 lie on the anchor b1, their peaks at the anchor’s width. Each node’s quantile map is pulled toward the batch-wide map (shrink_k = 1000, so small nodes borrow most). The pull is toward the batch-wide map evaluated at the node’s own values (shrink_target = "value"), so a stretch or compression shared by all nodes, as in b2 and b3, is kept. A smaller shrink_k trusts each node’s own map more.

study <- is.na(samples$reference_id[match(cells$sample_id, samples$sample_id)])
colours <- c(b1 = "black", b2 = "#E69F00", b3 = "#0072B2")
op <- par(mfrow = c(1, 2), mar = c(4, 4, 2, 1))
for (panel in c("uncorrected", "corrected")) {
  value <- if (panel == "uncorrected") cells$M else res$x$M
  plot(NULL, xlim = c(-0.5, 3.5), ylim = c(0, 1.6), xlab = "M", ylab = "Density", main = panel)
  for (b in names(colours)) {
    lines(density(value[study & cells$batch == b]), col = colours[[b]], lwd = 1.5)
  }
  legend("topright", legend = names(colours), col = colours, lwd = 1.5, bty = "n")
}






par(op)

Quantile-map plots
The quantile maps are the second step of the correction. For each second-pass node, a batch’s quantiles of M after the pass-1 shift (x axis) are mapped onto the anchor’s (y axis). A map on the diagonal changes nothing; a map steeper than the diagonal stretches, as for the compressed batch b2, and a flatter one compresses, as for the stretched batch b3. The anchor’s own map is the diagonal.

key_batch <- sub("\r.*", "", names(model$quantiles))
key_node <- sub(".*\r", "", names(model$quantiles))
op <- par(mfrow = c(1, length(unique(key_node))), mar = c(4, 4, 2, 1))
for (node in unique(key_node)) {
  anchor_q <- model$quantiles[[which(key_batch == "b1" & key_node == node)]][, "M"]
  node_q <- unlist(lapply(model$quantiles[key_node == node], function(q) q[, "M"]))
  plot(NULL, xlim = range(node_q), ylim = range(anchor_q),
    xlab = "Batch quantiles of M", ylab = "Anchor quantiles of M", main = node)
  abline(0, 1, col = "grey70", lty = 2)
  for (b in names(colours)) {
    i <- which(key_batch == b & key_node == node)
    if (length(i) == 1) lines(model$quantiles[[i]][, "M"], anchor_q, col = colours[[b]], lwd = 1.5, type = "b", pch = 20)
  }
}
legend("topleft", legend = names(colours), col = colours, lwd = 1.5, bty = "n")






par(op)

Error against the truth
In real data the truth is unknown, and the held-out bridge wells take its place (see the comparison article). Here each study cell’s value without the batch effect is known.

error <- data.frame(
  batch = cells$batch[study],
  uncorrected = abs(cells$M[study] - cells$truth[study]),
  corrected = abs(res$x$M[study] - cells$truth[study])
)
aggregate(cbind(uncorrected, corrected) ~ batch, data = error, FUN = mean)
#>   batch uncorrected    corrected
#> 1    b1   0.0000000 4.440892e-18
#> 2    b2   0.3544671 3.833640e-02
#> 3    b3   0.2534930 3.357202e-02

Earth mover’s distance between batches
The earth mover’s distance (EMD) between two batches’ distributions of a marker is 0 when they match. For the study cells of each batch against the anchor:

emd <- function(a, b) mean(abs(quantile(a, ppoints(200)) - quantile(b, ppoints(200))))
sapply(c(b2 = "b2", b3 = "b3"), function(b) {
  c(
    uncorrected = emd(cells$M[study & cells$batch == b], cells$M[study & cells$batch == "b1"]),
    corrected = emd(res$x$M[study & cells$batch == b], res$x$M[study & cells$batch == "b1"])
  )
})
#>                     b2         b3
#> uncorrected 0.34737481 0.11756999
#> corrected   0.03403882 0.03111684

Use case 3: Correct later batches with a frozen model: longitudinal studies where batches arrive over time.

title: bridgenorm 1.1.0
text:
bn_fit() now defaults to shrink_target = "value" and shrink_k = 1000 (1.0.0: "quantile" and 300). Corrected values change for every fit that relied on the defaults; pass shrink_target = "quantile", shrink_k = 300 to reproduce 1.0.0. Models saved by 1.0.0 still load and apply unchanged.
The new defaults were chosen by tuning on two real multi-batch cytometry studies, scored by the earth mover’s distance between batches on held-out bridge wells. The comparison used every fold, including those used to pick the settings, so the gain is an upper bound. Check the defaults on new data.
settings$shrink_target is now always recorded. A model without it used "quantile".





bn_fit(shrink_target = ): "value" shrinks each node’s offset curve toward the batch-wide map evaluated at the node’s own target quantiles, so an intensity-dependent effect shared by all nodes is not shrunk toward a wrong curve. "quantile" keeps the 1.0.0 rule.
bn_fit(shrink_reweight = TRUE) computes the batch-wide curve with weights that give each batch the target’s cell-state mix of bridge cells. Default FALSE.
bn_fit(quantile_maps = FALSE) keeps no quantile tables, so every cell takes the pass-2 node shift (an ablation). Default TRUE.

title: bridgenorm 1.1.0
text:
bn_fit() now defaults to shrink_target = "value" and shrink_k = 1000 (1.0.0: "quantile" and 300). Corrected values change for every fit that relied on the defaults; pass shrink_target = "quantile", shrink_k = 300 to reproduce 1.0.0. Models saved by 1.0.0 still load and apply unchanged.
The new defaults were chosen by tuning on two real multi-batch cytometry studies, scored by the earth mover’s distance between batches on held-out bridge wells. The comparison used every fold, including those used to pick the settings, so the gain is an upper bound. Check the defaults on new data.
settings$shrink_target is now always recorded. A model without it used "quantile".

title: bridgenorm 1.1.0
text:
bn_fit(shrink_target = ): "value" shrinks each node’s offset curve toward the batch-wide map evaluated at the node’s own target quantiles, so an intensity-dependent effect shared by all nodes is not shrunk toward a wrong curve. "quantile" keeps the 1.0.0 rule.
bn_fit(shrink_reweight = TRUE) computes the batch-wide curve with weights that give each batch the target’s cell-state mix of bridge cells. Default FALSE.
bn_fit(quantile_maps = FALSE) keeps no quantile tables, so every cell takes the pass-2 node shift (an ablation). Default TRUE.

title: bridgenorm 1.1.0
text:
Breaking changes

Models saved by 0.x do not load; refit them. Schema strings are now bn_node_quantile_model/2, bn_node_model/2 and bn_paired_model/2.
Every model has the parent class bn_model. bn_fit_paired() returns class c("bn_paired_model", "bn_model") (was bn_model).
bn_fit() drops the single-valued arguments method, eb_settings, assignment and tail. Their values are fixed and still recorded in settings.
In the actions of a bn_fit() result, the SOM node column is node (was population).
Dead fields are removed: hierarchy from paired models, the duplicate global model from node models, eb_settings and assignment from node settings.
seed must be a whole number. kohonen moves from Suggests to Imports.

title: bridgenorm 1.1.0
text:
New

goal_batches: with target = "virtual", bn_fit() and bn_fit_paired() map every batch toward the equal-weight mean of a chosen set of batches, for example the batches of one study, as CytoNorm’s goal distribution. Unbridged or donor-mismatched goal batches are dropped; a goal lacking a reference summary the anchor has stops the fit. No benchmark benefit is claimed yet.
bn_fit() warns when a batch gets no quantile maps (donors that pass min_cells differ from the anchor’s) and when bridge donors’ cell shares differ from the anchor’s by more than 10 percentage points.
bn_apply() sends a message naming batches it left entirely raw.

title: bridgenorm 1.1.0
text:
Fixes

bn_apply() no longer stops when a marker has one value in a node’s quantile table: that marker keeps the pass-2 node shift (reason code node_quantile_tied).
An empty or blank sample_id, batch, reference_id or aliquot, and carriage returns in ids or population labels, now stop with the samples named. Before, "" silently made study samples a bridge donor.
Quantile tables are built only for batches whose aliquots pass min_cells, the gate the shift passes use.
The fit no longer depends on the collation locale or on the session’s RNG kind. Results on data whose ids sort the same in every locale are unchanged.
The digest leaves out timestamps and hashes a canonical form, so two fits on the same data have the same digest.
bn_reference_noise() takes transform as optional. Choice errors name the function the user called. bn_load() checks that the file exists.

title: bridgenorm
text:
For each batch, population and marker, the effect is the mean over the references shared with the anchor batch of (reference summary in the batch minus the same reference’s summary in the anchor). Reference summaries are equal-weight means of aliquot means. Nothing is shrunk. This is the baseline every bridgenorm model must beat, the estimator bn_fit uses in each SOM node, and the one bn_apply uses for batches unseen at fit time.

bn_fit_paired(
  x,
  samples,
  population,
  markers,
  transform,
  anchor,
  min_cells = 50,
  unbridged = "abstain",
  target = "anchor",
  goal_batches = NULL,
  sample_ids = NULL
)





x


A numeric matrix (cells by markers) or a data frame with one row per cell, already transformed. A data frame needs a sample_id column unless sample_ids is given.




samples


Data frame, one row per sample: sample_id, batch, reference_id (the bridge donor; NA for study samples) and optionally aliquot.




population


Per-cell population labels, one per row of x, frozen before correction.




markers


Marker columns to correct.




transform


list(name = “asinh”, cofactor = <number>): the scale x is on. It is recorded, never applied.




anchor


The batch that defines the target scale.




min_cells


Minimum cells per reference aliquot summary and per (batch, node) quantile table.




unbridged


“abstain” leaves a batch that shares no bridge donor with the anchor raw and flags it; “stop” refuses the fit.




target


“anchor” corrects every batch to the anchor batch. “virtual” replaces each anchor reference summary by its mean over the bridged batches, so the anchor batch gets an effect too. The anchor still sets the bridges.




goal_batches


NULL, or with target = “virtual” two or more batches whose equal-weight mean is the goal (for example the batches of one study), as CytoNorm’s goal distribution. Goal batches that are unbridged or whose reference donors differ from the anchor’s are dropped. The anchor still sets the bridges and the map and may lie outside the goal; the fit stops when the goal lacks a reference summary the anchor has. Nodes without a goal quantile table take the pass-2 node shift.




sample_ids


Optional sample id per row; required for a matrix x.



se_donor is the SD of the paired differences over references divided by the square root of their number (NA with one reference), with df = number of references - 1. Anchor rows have estimate 0 and support = “anchor”. With target = “virtual” each reference summary of the anchor is replaced by its mean over the bridged batches, so the anchor batch gets an effect too.
With unbridged = “abstain”, a batch that shares no reference with the anchor (after min_cells) gets no effect, so bn_apply leaves its cells raw and flags them; “stop” refuses the fit.

A bn_model: a list with method = “paired_shift”, settings, markers, transform, anchor, effects (one row per batch, population and marker: estimate, se_donor, df, donor and aliquot counts, support), targets (anchor summaries), bridges, excluded, known_batches and digest.

bn_fit, bn_apply


library("bridgenorm")

set.seed(1)
batches <- c("b1", "b2", "b3")
samples <- expand.grid(donor = c("D1", "D2"), batch = batches, stringsAsFactors = FALSE)
samples$sample_id <- paste(samples$donor, samples$batch, sep = "_")
samples$reference_id <- samples$donor
shift <- c(b1 = 0, b2 = 0.5, b3 = -0.3)
x <- do.call(rbind, lapply(seq_len(nrow(samples)), function(i) {
  data.frame(
    sample_id = samples$sample_id[i],
    Lin = rnorm(100, 2 + shift[[samples$batch[i]]], 0.3)
  )
}))
model <- bn_fit_paired(
  x, samples, population = rep("T", nrow(x)), markers = "Lin",
  transform = list(name = "asinh", cofactor = 5), anchor = "b1",
  min_cells = 20
)
model$effects[, c("batch", "estimate", "se_donor")]

  batch estimate se_donor
  <chr>    <dbl>    <dbl>
1 b1       0       0     
2 b2       0.502   0.0253
3 b3      -0.323   0.0212

title: bridgenorm
text:
bn_save() checks the digest and writes the model with saveRDS(). bn_load() reads it and checks the schema and digest again, so a changed file fails to load.

bn_save(model, path)

bn_load(path)





model


A bn_model, bn_node_model or bn_node_quantile_model.




path


File path.



bn_save() returns path invisibly; bn_load() returns the model.


library("bridgenorm")

# Two batches, each with two bridge wells of one reference donor and one
# study sample. Marker M is shifted by 0.5 in batch b2; Lin separates two
# cell states.
set.seed(1)
samples <- data.frame(
  sample_id = c("r1_b1", "r2_b1", "s_b1", "r1_b2", "r2_b2", "s_b2"),
  batch = rep(c("b1", "b2"), each = 3),
  reference_id = rep(c("donor", "donor", NA), 2),
  aliquot = rep(c("a1", "a2", NA), 2)
)
x <- do.call(rbind, lapply(seq_len(nrow(samples)), function(i) {
  shift <- if (samples$batch[i] == "b2") 0.5 else 0
  data.frame(
    sample_id = samples$sample_id[i],
    Lin = c(rnorm(200, 1, 0.2), rnorm(200, 4, 0.2)),
    M = c(rnorm(200, 2, 0.3), rnorm(200, 1, 0.3)) + shift
  )
}))
model <- bn_fit(
  x, samples, population = rep("T", nrow(x)), markers = c("Lin", "M"),
  transform = list(name = "asinh", cofactor = 5), anchor = "b1",
  grid = c(2, 1), mapping_markers = "Lin", seed = 1, rlen = 20
)
path <- tempfile(fileext = ".rds")
bn_save(model, path)
identical(bn_load(path)$digest, model$digest)

[1] TRUE

title: bridgenorm
text:
Corrects x with the frozen effects and reports one action per (batch, population, marker). Earlier effects never change, so values corrected before stay the same when new batches arrive.

bn_apply(
  model,
  x,
  samples,
  population,
  transform = model\$transform,
  unsupported = "abstain",
  sample_ids = NULL
)





model


A model from bn_fit or bn_fit_paired.




x


Data in the same form as for bn_fit.




samples


Sample table covering every sample in x.




population


Per-cell population labels for x.




transform


The scale x is on; it must equal the model’s. Defaults to the model’s own transform.




unsupported


“abstain” keeps uncorrectable values and reports them; “error” stops when any action is an abstention.




sample_ids


Optional sample id per row; required for a matrix x.



Arrival cases:


Known batch


Use the frozen effect. Reference samples in x are not used again.


New batch with a bridging reference


A reference in the new batch also has a frozen summary in the anchor batch. Its effect is the mean paired difference of its own reference cells to the frozen anchor summaries, without shrinkage. The effect is added to a copy of the model (returned as model); old effects are untouched.


New batch without a bridging reference


Abstain.


Known batch or population without an effect


Abstain. This covers batches dropped by unbridged = “abstain”.


Abstain keeps the original value exactly.

A bn_result: a list with x (corrected data, same shape, row order and columns as the input), actions (one row per batch, population and marker: action, reason_code, reason, estimate and support columns, n_cells), model (the input model, or a copy extended with new-batch effects, with a new digest and parent_digest), excluded and aliquot_source.

bn_fit


library("bridgenorm")

# Two batches, each with two bridge wells of one reference donor and one
# study sample. Marker M is shifted by 0.5 in batch b2; Lin separates two
# cell states.
set.seed(1)
samples <- data.frame(
  sample_id = c("r1_b1", "r2_b1", "s_b1", "r1_b2", "r2_b2", "s_b2"),
  batch = rep(c("b1", "b2"), each = 3),
  reference_id = rep(c("donor", "donor", NA), 2),
  aliquot = rep(c("a1", "a2", NA), 2)
)
x <- do.call(rbind, lapply(seq_len(nrow(samples)), function(i) {
  shift <- if (samples$batch[i] == "b2") 0.5 else 0
  data.frame(
    sample_id = samples$sample_id[i],
    Lin = c(rnorm(200, 1, 0.2), rnorm(200, 4, 0.2)),
    M = c(rnorm(200, 2, 0.3), rnorm(200, 1, 0.3)) + shift
  )
}))
model <- bn_fit(
  x, samples, population = rep("T", nrow(x)), markers = c("Lin", "M"),
  transform = list(name = "asinh", cofactor = 5), anchor = "b1",
  grid = c(2, 1), mapping_markers = "Lin", seed = 1, rlen = 20
)
res <- bn_apply(model, x, samples, rep("T", nrow(x)))
res
